reference.source: WHO Classification of Head and Neck Tumours
clinicalPearls: A benign monomorphic adenoma composed of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and a distinct basement-membrane-like rim, most commonly in the parotid.
The defining negative feature is the absence of the chondromyxoid stroma of pleomorphic adenoma, which aids histological distinction.
Recognised architectural subtypes are solid, trabecular, tubular and membranous.
The membranous (dermal analogue) subtype is associated with Brooke-Spiegler syndrome, with synchronous cutaneous cylindromas and trichoepitheliomas and germline CYLD alteration.
Non-membranous subtypes frequently harbour CTNNB1 (beta-catenin) mutations, with nuclear beta-catenin accumulation on immunohistochemistry.
It typically presents in older adults as a slow-growing, mobile, painless mass with a slight female predominance.
The membranous subtype is more often multifocal and recurs more readily than other subtypes.
A basaloid aspirate on cytology overlaps substantially with adenoid cystic carcinoma, so caution is needed before a benign report.
reference.pathophysiology: Basal cell adenoma is a benign epithelial neoplasm arising from the basal reserve cells of the salivary duct system, showing both luminal ductal and abluminal (basal/myoepithelial) differentiation but lacking the mesenchymal-type chondromyxoid matrix of pleomorphic adenoma. In most non-membranous tumours, activating mutations in CTNNB1 lead to nuclear translocation of beta-catenin and constitutive WNT pathway signalling, promoting basaloid proliferation. The membranous subtype is genetically distinct, associated with inactivation of the CYLD tumour suppressor in the context of Brooke-Spiegler syndrome, which predisposes to multiple adnexal and salivary basaloid tumours. Growth is expansile and encapsulated in most subtypes, although the membranous type is characteristically multinodular and less well demarcated.
additionalInvestigations: Fine-needle aspiration cytology, with core biopsy if a basaloid lesion is uncertain
MRI for well-defined lesions and to assess extent
Immunohistochemistry including beta-catenin and myoepithelial markers
Examination and history for cutaneous cylindromas or trichoepitheliomas (Brooke-Spiegler syndrome)
Histological examination of the excised specimen
redFlags: Infiltrative or ill-defined margins suggesting basal cell adenocarcinoma
Perineural symptoms such as numbness or facial weakness pointing towards adenoid cystic carcinoma
Multifocal tumours with syndromic cutaneous features
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent after complete excision for non-membranous subtypes, with malignant transformation rare. The membranous subtype has a higher rate of local recurrence and multicentricity and warrants closer follow-up.
pitfalls: Misclassifying a basaloid aspirate as adenoid cystic carcinoma or vice versa
Failing to identify the underlying Brooke-Spiegler syndrome in membranous tumours
Mistaking an infiltrative basal cell adenocarcinoma for a benign adenoma
Assuming complete excision without recognising the multifocality of the membranous subtype
